awd_titl_txt: Conference: National Ambient Energy for Buildings Research Symposium (NAEBRS)
awd_abstract_narration:
This grant is in partial support of a three-day symposium to identify research gaps and needs for ambient energy buildings. The symposium is targeted to be held in the fall of 2025 at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico. Ghost Ranch is a historic and fitting location for this ambient energy focused event, as the site includes passive solar cabins. Registration will be limited to approximately 55 in-person and 30 virtual participants from all facets of building research, education, policy, and industry. Ambient energy for buildings offers promising contributions for handling energy challenges. Much of the energy use in homes is directed towards maintaining comfortable temperatures, such as heating and cooling, and ambient energy approaches address both these functions. Moreover, regular household activities like hot water, lighting, refrigeration, and cooking can be powered more sustainably with ambient approaches. The abundant energy offered by the natural environment—sourced from the sun, wind, sky and earth—holds untapped potential. Further, by weaving in natural light and designs inspired by nature, living spaces can be transformed into more comfortable and health-promoting environments. Ambient-conditioned buildings can serve not only as a cornerstone for architectural advancement but can also significantly contribute to environmental sustainability, societal well-being, and educational development. The symposium aims to be a hub of innovation, bringing together luminaries from diverse fields such as architecture, design, engineering, and education. Anticipated key outcomes of the symposium include (1) a roadmap for integrating ambient energy and passive solar into modern building practices, (2) cross-disciplinary collaborations formed to spearhead new projects and research in the field, (3) a collection of best practices, case studies, and recommendations to guide policymakers and industry leaders in adopting sustainable practices, and (4) a website that will serve as a hub that houses the items just listed.

The 21st century presents a dual mandate: to counteract climate change and ensure the wellbeing of the global populace. A pivotal player in this scenario is the building sector. The startling fact is that in the US, buildings dominate energy consumption charts, utilizing a significant proportion of electricity and natural gas. Their contribution to carbon emissions is also high. To tackle climate change effectively, there must be a focus on the building sector. While there has been enthusiasm about turning buildings "green" and achieving net-zero standards, the transition is moving more slowly than expected. Projections suggest that by the mid-century, a substantial portion of electricity will still be tied to fossil fuels. And, with urban sprawl and increasing infrastructure, building footprint is set to expand, potentially exacerbating the fossil fuel conundrum. This necessitates a rethinking of the current approach, expanding it to more fully embrace ambient energy for buildings.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The National Ambient Energy for Buildings Research Symposium (NAEBRS) brought together researchers, architects, engineers, builders, educators, policy specialists, and other professionals to examine how naturally available energy from the sun, sky, air, and ground can reduce the energy required to operate buildings. The symposium was held September 7–10, 2025, and included 50 presentations as well as building tours, demonstrations, discussions, and opportunities for participants to exchange ideas.

An important outcome of the project was connecting the historical knowledge of pioneers in passive solar and climate-responsive building design with current research and practice. Several leaders who helped establish the field participated in the symposium and shared lessons from decades of research, design, construction, and building operation. Their perspectives were combined with presentations on contemporary technologies, materials, modeling approaches, and design strategies. This exchange preserved valuable knowledge from earlier generations while providing a foundation for continued innovation.

The symposium demonstrated the wide range of ways that ambient energy can contribute to building performance. Presentations and discussions addressed passive and active solar heating, nighttime and radiative cooling, ground-based heating and cooling approaches, high-performance building envelopes and windows, thermal storage materials, solar water heating and cooking, daylighting, and other applications. Case studies showed how these strategies can be incorporated into both new and existing buildings and can function in different climates. Participants also examined building resilience during extreme weather and power outages.

The project extended beyond building technologies themselves. Sessions considered computer-based design tools, education and outreach, building codes and standards, public policy, and social factors that influence adoption. These topics emphasized that broader use of ambient energy depends not only on technical advances but also on making information and design methods accessible to building professionals and the public.

A broader outcome of NAEBRS was the creation and strengthening of connections among people working in areas that are often treated separately. Researchers and practitioners were able to compare experiences, identify opportunities for collaboration, and discuss future directions for ambient-energy buildings. The symposium concluded with a group discussion devoted specifically to actions that could advance the field.

The project also established mechanisms for extending its impact beyond those who attended the symposium. Symposium information and presentations are being preserved as publicly accessible resources, allowing educators, researchers, building professionals, students, and members of the public to benefit from the material. Participants also continued dissemination through activities such as a post-symposium webinar and development of a special journal issue focused on ambient energy for buildings.

Ultimately, the project highlighted the potential for buildings to make greater use of energy that is already available in their surroundings. By reducing dependence on purchased energy for heating, cooling, lighting, water heating, and other needs, ambient-energy strategies can contribute to lower energy demand, improved resilience, and more sustainable and comfortable buildings. NAEBRS helped preserve important knowledge from the field's history while connecting it with current research and creating resources and relationships that can support future progress.
